source.title: CoE: Chain-of-Explanation via Automatic Visual Concept Circuit Description and Polysemanticity Quantification
source.authors: Wen-Long Yu; Qi-Long Wang; Chuang Liu; Dong Li; Qing-Hua Hu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures semantic concept diversity in deep vision models, but does not test feature overlap, sparse co-activation, limited representational capacity, or the geometric directions described in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's CPE results concern counts and distributions of language-described semantic atoms assigned to vision-model channels. They do not measure neural feature directions or establish that semantic multiplicity arises from capacity pressure. Local-explanation score comparisons and method performance are not results on the claim's superposition mechanism.
record.test_reason: The paper measures how diverse the LVLM-generated word labels are for top-relevance image patches of vision-model channels (ResNet, CLIP-ResNet50). It cites Toy Models only in passing. It does not measure feature directions, sparsity, capacity or SAE features, and does not study LLMs, so no version is tested. Channel polysemanticity in vision models is related to V2–V4, but this label-diversity entropy cannot separate superposition from other causes. It is not evidence for or against any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that polysemanticity is lowest in shallow and deep layers, peaks in intermediate layers, and rises with model depth, which they read as more complex models being harder to interpret. They make no claim about superposition or capacity.
record.recipe_differences: No superposition method is reproduced or adapted; the paper uses post-hoc visual concept extraction, language-described semantic atoms, and CPE.
record.method_sensitivity: CPE trends differ by XAI method; the reported CPE patterns also vary across model depth, layer, and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet152, LVLM-labelled channel concepts average 12.7–18.3 distinct semantic atoms, depending on stage. Label entropy (CPE) peaks at stage 3 and rises with ResNet depth under relevance-based extraction, but falls with depth under activation-based extraction. CLIP-ResNet50 scores higher than ResNet50. CPE agrees with human pairwise judgments 75% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision-model channels show language-label polysemanticity that varies by layer, depth and architecture, and its measured trend depends on the concept-extraction method.

record.problems: The measured polysemanticity is operationalized through LVLM-generated linguistic atoms and post-hoc concept extraction, rather than direct neural-feature geometry or activation sparsity. The text gives no uncertainty estimates for the CPE results or the 75% agreement figure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Explanation-quality comparisons are excluded because they evaluate CoE explanations, not superposition or the claim's capacity mechanism.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature/dimension ratios, sparsity transition or geometry.
Capacity competition is not tested. The authors' explanation of CLIP's higher CPE (wider semantic scope) is speculation, not a capacity test.
No mechanism for polysemanticity is isolated.
No LLMs; no measure of feature spread across neurons; no SAE recovery.

record.verdict_notes: CPE depends on a padding heuristic: without padding, uniform concepts score CPE=1. It also depends on GPT-4o labelling, a DeBERTa entailment clustering step, and the choice of XAI method. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Peer-reviewed at CVPR 2025.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-to-dimension ratios, sparse feature activations, overlapping neural directions, sparsity transitions, or regular geometries are tested.
The paper does not test whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.

It measures semantic diversity in vision-model channels but does not establish that polysemanticity arises through a mechanism other than superposition or show that it is not evidence of superposition.
The models studied are vision models, not LLMs; no feature spread across LLM neurons or SAE recovery is tested.
No SAE features are studied, and completeness, stability, or canonical status of dictionary features is not tested.
The paper's linguistic concept atoms are not neural representation directions; it does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Measured CPE across concepts in the selected output layers of four stages.
rows.measure: CPE by concept; reported range and qualitative distribution
rows.value: CPE ranges from a maximum of 1 to a minimum of 0.5; most concepts show a noticeable level of polysemanticity.
rows.note: This is the paper's semantic-atom CPE, not a measure of neural-direction overlap or feature sparsity.

rows.subject: ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Compared averaged CPE across four selected layers.

conditions.value: output layer of each of stages 1–4

rows.value: Averaged CPE peaks in stage 3; the shallowest and deepest layers have lower values.
rows.note: The text gives the ordering but no exact layer values.

rows.subject: ResNet50, ResNet101, ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Compared averaged CPE across models of different depths.
rows.value: CPE shows a rising trend as the number of layers increases.
rows.note: The text reports a trend, not exact values.

rows.subject: ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Counted distinct concept atoms after semantic clustering.
rows.measure: Average quantity of non-overlapping semantic atoms per concept
rows.value: 12.7 at the final layer and 18.3 at stage 3; stage 3 has the most and the final layer the fewest.
rows.note: The paper describes these as linguistic semantic atoms per concept, not neural directions.

rows.subject: ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Compared CPE computed from different visual-concept extraction methods.

conditions.value: relevance-based, activation-based, and maximum mutual information-based

rows.measure: CPE trends across methods and model complexity
rows.value: Activation-based CPE diminishes as model complexity increases, unlike the trend for relevance-based CPE; maximum-mutual-information concepts have lower CPE values.
rows.note: The authors state that the choice of XAI method is critical; no exact values are given in the text.
rows.check: The CPE trend changes direction with the XAI method (activation-based vs relevance-based). This shows the depth trend in r3 depends on method; the row is better read as method sensitivity than as a finding.

rows.subject: CLIP-ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Compared averaged CPE across model architectures and stages.
rows.measure: CPE by stage and whole model
rows.value: The CLIP vision branch exhibits greater polysemanticity; its general trend is lowest at abstract stage 4 and peaks in intermediate stages, with high polysemanticity in the shallowest stage.
rows.note: The authors suggest the OOD ImageNet Validation data used to construct concepts and CLIP's training-data scope as possible explanations.

rows.subject: ResNet152
rows.operation_detail: Compared CPE rankings with human pairwise judgments of visual-concept polysemanticity.

conditions.value: 10 groups, each evaluated by three participants

rows.measure: Agreement between CPE and human assessments
rows.note: The result assesses agreement for this semantic-atom metric, not agreement about neural superposition.
rows.check: This row validates the authors' own CPE metric against human judgments. It is a measure-validation result, not a result on polysemanticity or superposition, so it should be flagged as method evaluation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
